::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Essay, November 2026.** A short, philosophical essay on what AI means for discovery and for learning. It starts from Poincaré's view that scientists pursue the harmony they sense in nature [@poincare1914], Iain McGilchrist's claim that great discoveries are not made by following the scientific method [@mcgilchrist2026], and Terence Tao's recent warnings about AI in mathematics [@tao2026blog; @tao2026scifri]. The one figure is a schematic of my own, drawn with the code in [figs.py](figs.py).
:::

**In short.** Ask an AI what to try next in research, and it will give a sensible answer, close to what the field already believes. That is the scientific method, perfected: rank ideas by how plausible they look, test the best first. But the discoveries that change a field often looked least plausible, and their evidence came only after years of work that seemed to lead nowhere. Reaching them takes two things the method does not hold: taste, a sense that an unlikely idea is beautiful enough to be true, and faith, the will to stay with it in the dark. Taste is not given. It is grown on the path: the failed attempts, the partial results, the slow understanding of why. AI now walks more of that path for us, and mathematics shows both the gain and the cost. Part of the path was only toil, and we can let it go. The part where understanding is made we need to keep, and that means reinventing how we learn along it.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" icon="false"}
## Key takeaways

- AI ranks ideas the way a field already does, faster and more evenly than any of us. That is the method, perfected.
- Great discoveries tend to rank last: implausible to experts, silent for years before the evidence comes.
- What carries them through is taste and faith. Faith without taste is only stubbornness.
- Taste grows on the path. If AI reaches the results and we skip the walk, we lose the faculty that tells us which unlikely idea to believe in.
- Not all of the path matters. We should let the toil go, keep the part where understanding is made, and reinvent how we learn it.
:::

## 1. The best rule-follower ever made

Ask a capable model what to try next in a research programme, and the answer will be good: well argued, well referenced, and close to what the field already believes. This is not a flaw. The model learned from what the field has written, and it was rewarded for answers experts rate as good.

This is also what we were taught the scientific method is: careful rules, reduction to parts, plausible hypotheses tested in order. If that were the whole of science, AI would soon be its best practitioner, and some systems already try to run the whole loop, from idea to paper [@lu2024].

I think AI is something more precise than a new scientist. It is the method, perfected. It ranks the world by what we already find plausible, and it will make us much faster at that. Which raises two questions. What about the discoveries that were never plausible? And what happens to us, if we stop walking the path that taught us to see them?

## 2. The ideas the method ranks last

In the early 1980s, Barry Marshall and Robin Warren proposed that a bacterium causes stomach ulcers. Most experts believed that bacteria could not live in the acid of the stomach. Their paper met disbelief [@marshall1984], and Marshall ended up drinking a culture of the bacterium to show that it made him ill. They received the Nobel Prize in 2005. In the same years, Dan Shechtman saw a crystal pattern the textbooks said could not exist [@shechtman1984]. For years he was told he was wrong. He received the Nobel Prize in 2011.

The pattern has names. Thomas Kuhn distinguished puzzle-solving inside a shared frame from the revolutions that change the frame [@kuhn1962]. A saying attributed to Max Planck holds that science advances one funeral at a time, and economists have found that when a star scientist dies, outsiders do enter the field and publish work that is cited more [@azoulay2019]. Highly novel papers are more likely to end up among the most cited, but they are recognised late [@wang2017].

What these stories share is a stretch of time I think of as the dark period. The idea is on the table, but the decisive evidence is years away. In between, the signals are weak and often discouraging. A careful person, following the rules, would move on.

![**Figure 1.** An idea the field expects gathers evidence quickly. An idea it does not expect goes through a dark period, where the evidence wanders and often falls below the point where a careful method would move on. Only someone who keeps going reaches the test. Schematic, my own.](figures/fig01.svg){fig-alt="A chart of evidence for an idea against time spent on it. A blue curve, an idea the consensus expects, rises quickly and levels off. It dips below a red dashed line labelled below this line, the method moves on. Then it rises steeply above the blue curve after the dark period ends. A label says conviction carries it to the decisive test."}

Give that careful person an AI, and they can work further down the list of ideas, faster. But it is the same list, in the same order, because the list is the field's own sense of what is plausible. AI moves the method along the consensus. It does not move it across.

## 3. Beauty as a sieve

So what makes someone stay with an idea through the dark? Poincaré answered more than a century ago. The scientist, he wrote, "does not study nature because it is useful to do so. He studies it because he takes pleasure in it, and he takes pleasure in it because it is beautiful" [@poincare1914, Book I, ch. 1]. He meant the harmony among the parts, which the mind grasps. Among the countless combinations an inventor could try, he argued, a sense of elegance acts as a sieve, letting through the few worth checking [@poincare1914, Book I, ch. 3].

Michael Polanyi said something similar: all knowing involves personal commitment, and "intellectual passions" decide which problems are worth a life [@polanyi1958]. Iain McGilchrist argues that the great advances came from breaking the rules rather than following them, and from seeing the world whole rather than only in parts [@mcgilchrist2026]. I share his conclusion, without needing his account of the brain's two hemispheres, which is debated.

Taste, in this sense, is a signal the literature does not contain. If it were written down, it would already be part of the consensus, and the method would use it. Which raises the question the rest of this essay turns on: if taste is not in the books, where does it come from?

## 4. Where taste is grown

My answer is that taste is grown on the path. It comes from the attempts that failed, the lemma that almost worked, the example that broke the rule, the slow sense of why one approach goes somewhere and another does not. Nobody can hand it over, because it is not a result. It is what the search leaves in the searcher.

Mathematics is where this is now being tested in public. AI systems are producing proofs and settling problems that stayed open for years. Terence Tao, who has used these tools as much as anyone, has warned that something is being lost. As I read him, his point is that AI can reach a famous result without the understanding that made it worth reaching, and that the scarce step in mathematics is moving from finding proofs to explaining them [@tao2026scifri]. In a recent post he goes further: if machines do the work and people stop practising real understanding, even our checks on the machines may become illusions, and understanding becomes a public good that nobody is paid to produce [@tao2026blog].

I believe this is the deepest risk of all, deeper than ranking great ideas last. If we skip the path, we do not only learn less. We stop growing the very faculty that lets anyone believe in an unlikely idea for good reasons. Faith without taste is stubbornness. A generation that has the answers without the walk may keep its faith and lose its taste.

The evidence from learning points the same way. High-school students who practised mathematics with an unrestricted chatbot did better while they had it, and worse than others once it was taken away [@bastani2025]. The effort was where the skill formed.

But I do not think the whole path is sacred, and here I want to argue against myself. Mathematics has lost parts of its path before. Nobody mourns tables of logarithms or pages of hand calculation. When Appel and Haken proved the four colour theorem with a computer in 1976 [@appel1977], many complained that it explained nothing, and mathematicians kept looking for why it was true. Understanding came after the answer, and the answer gave the search a destination. In Go, after superhuman programs appeared, professional players began making better and more novel moves [@shin2023]. They lost part of the old path and found a higher one.

So the honest version of the claim is narrower than "the path matters most". Part of the path is toil, and we can let machines take it. Part of the path is where understanding is made, and that part we are about to lose by accident, because it looks like toil from outside.

## 5. Faith, narrowly

The word faith makes scientists uneasy, so let me say what I mean. Faith here is belief in an idea beyond what the evidence yet supports, together with the will to act on it for a long time. It is closer to Polanyi's commitment than to religion.

The strongest objection is obvious. For every Marshall, many people believed against the evidence and were simply wrong. Survivors tell the story; the others are forgotten. I accept this. Most faith in science is misplaced, and that is exactly why it needs taste.

But the argument does not need believers to be right most of the time. It needs only this: without them, the right few are never tested. A field where nobody spends years on an idea the field doubts will never find out which of those ideas were true.

My real claim is a belief, not a result. I suspect that, at the edges of every field, the consensus is wrong in a systematic way: some kinds of far-fetched ideas turn out true more often than experts expect, and nothing written beforehand tells which. If so, no amount of better ranking reaches them. Only someone who believes first does, and only someone who has walked enough of the path believes in the right ones.

## 6. Could cheap testing make faith unnecessary?

There is a serious way this could fail, and it comes from AI itself. Faith matters because testing is expensive. If testing an idea became nearly free, we would test everything, and the unlikely ideas would be checked along with the rest. Call it a singularity of discovery: search so cheap that ranking, and faith, stop mattering.

In some places this may already be happening. In games, code, mathematics with proof checkers, protein structure, the goal is fixed and an answer can be checked in seconds. There machines have already gone beyond the consensus: AlphaGo's successors played moves no strong human would have played [@silver2017], and AlphaTensor found ways to multiply matrices that people had missed [@fawzi2022].

Open science is different, for three reasons. The space of ideas grows with knowledge: every answer opens new questions. Many tests have a physical pace that computation cannot shorten, such as a ten-year trial, a new instrument, or a field's slow change of mind. And only ideas someone proposes ever get tested. Experts rated research ideas from a language model as more novel than their own, yet the model's ideas varied little from one to the next [@si2025]. If the far ideas never enter the queue, cheap testing never reaches them.

And notice what even the fast domains show. Where machines find answers by the thousand, the scarce thing becomes understanding them, which is Tao's point. Cheap testing does not remove the need for the path. It moves it from finding to understanding.

## 7. Reinventing the path

AI is a mirror: it shows how much of what we called research was search and checking inside a frame. It is a risk of convergence: when everyone consults the same models, each researcher improves while the field narrows. Scientists who use AI publish more and are cited more, while AI-heavy research covers a narrower range of topics [@hao2024], and writers helped by AI write better stories that resemble each other more [@doshi2024]. And it is an opportunity, if we change how we learn along the way.

Here is what that could mean, for students and for working researchers alike:

1. **Try first, then ask.** Make your own attempt before opening the tool, so the machine corrects your path instead of replacing it.
2. **Answer first, then walk.** When AI gives a result, treat it as a known destination and derive it yourself. Knowing it is true removes the fear of a dead end and keeps the learning.
3. **Explanation as the deliverable.** A result is not done until a person can say why it is true, in their own words, to someone else.
4. **A checker, not a writer.** Proof assistants and tests can check each step you write without writing it for you, like a tutor who only says "not yet".
5. **Pay for understanding.** If understanding has become a public good, institutions must reward it: exposition, teaching, the second and clearer proof, not only the first result.
6. **Keep one idea of your own.** Something you find beautiful and nobody else believes yet. Expect to be wrong most of the time.

None of these refuses the tool. They decide which part of the walk stays ours.

## 8. How I could be wrong, and what to do in the dark

Three things would prove this essay wrong. If the consensus is right even at its edges, faith is only a story we tell afterwards. If the signal that separates the right far ideas from the wrong ones is already in the literature, a good enough model will find it, and taste adds nothing. And if taste can be grown without walking, by studying machine solutions as chess players study engines, then the path matters less than I think. The first two could be checked by giving a model only the literature written before a past breakthrough, and seeing whether it would have dismissed the idea. The third we will learn from the next generation of students.

Until then, this is what I take from it. Let the machine do the search, the checking, the long list of plausible next steps. Walk part of the path yourself, on purpose, because that is where taste is grown. Then use that taste to choose one unlikely idea, and stay with it long enough to find out.

Machines can tell us what is likely. Deciding what is worth believing long enough to prove it is still up to us.
